statement:
Implement an in-memory reservation service. The service manages a fixed set of resources (meeting rooms, GPUs, and so on). Resource names are strings, given all at once in the constructor; none are added or removed later. Time is an integer (think of it as "minute number"). A booking occupies a half-open interval [start, end) on one resource.

The following rules apply to all three parts:

  • Intervals [a, b) and [c, d) overlap if and only if a < d and c < b. Touching end to end does not count as overlapping: [9, 11) and [11, 12) can coexist.
  • On the same resource, no two active bookings may overlap. Different resources are independent.
  • 0 <= start < end <= 10**9. Raise ValueError when start >= end, and KeyError when the resource name does not exist. A call that raises must not change any state. If both errors apply, raising either one is fine.
  • A successful booking returns a booking id. Ids start at 1 and increase by 1 with each success; failed calls do not consume an id.
  • owner is just a label and plays no part in any decision; anyone can cancel a booking by its id.

Part 1 — Single-threaded version

class ReservationService:
    def __init__(self, resources: list[str]): ...

    def reserve(self, resource: str, start: int, end: int, owner: str) -> int | None:
        """Book [start, end) on `resource`. Returns the new booking id,
        or None if it overlaps a booking that is already there."""

    def cancel(self, booking_id: int) -> bool:
        """True if the booking existed and is now cancelled.
        False if the id was never issued or is already cancelled."""

    def query(self, resource: str, start: int, end: int) -> list[tuple[int, int, int, str]]:
        """The bookings on `resource` that overlap [start, end),
        as (start, end, booking_id, owner), sorted by start."""

A resource may hold tens of thousands of bookings, so when reserve checks for a conflict it must not scan all of that resource's bookings; it should make only O(logn) comparisons (n is the number of active bookings on that resource).

svc = ReservationService(["room-a", "room-b"])
svc.reserve("room-a", 9, 11, "ann")     -> 1
svc.reserve("room-a", 11, 12, "bob")    -> 2       # [9,11) and [11,12) only touch end to end
svc.reserve("room-a", 10, 13, "cat")    -> None    # overlaps both 1 and 2
svc.reserve("room-b", 10, 13, "cat")    -> 3       # a different resource; the previous failure used no id
svc.query("room-a", 0, 24)              -> [(9, 11, 1, "ann"), (11, 12, 2, "bob")]
svc.query("room-a", 11, 12)             -> [(11, 12, 2, "bob")]
svc.query("room-a", 12, 24)             -> []
svc.cancel(1)                           -> True
svc.cancel(1)                           -> False   # already cancelled
svc.cancel(99)                          -> False   # an id that was never issued
svc.reserve("room-a", 10, 11, "cat")    -> 4
svc.query("room-a", 0, 24)              -> [(10, 11, 4, "cat"), (11, 12, 2, "bob")]
svc.reserve("room-c", 1, 2, "dan")      -> KeyError
svc.reserve("room-a", 5, 5, "dan")      -> ValueError

Part 2 — Many threads calling at once

Now many threads call reserve, cancel and query on the same object concurrently. The service as a whole must behave as if these calls ran one at a time in some order, and a call that starts after another call has returned must come after it and see all of its effects (this is called linearizable). Specifically:

  1. No double bookings. At any moment, the active bookings on one resource are pairwise non-overlapping. When several threads race for the same slot, exactly one gets an id and the rest get None.
  2. Ids are unique and have no gaps. If there were K successes in total, the ids issued are exactly 1..K.
  3. A cancel takes effect exactly once. When several threads cancel the same id at once, exactly one returns True. If a thread's cancel returns False because "someone else already cancelled it," then a reserve that starts after it returns must see the slot as free.
  4. A query is a snapshot. query returns a state that really existed at some moment, and the returned list is not affected by later operations.
  5. Different resources don't wait on each other. You may not wrap the whole of reserve in one global lock: later on the critical section may contain slow operations, such as writing to a database, and someone booking room A should not queue behind someone booking room B. A small lock that protects only very short operations, such as the id counter, is exempt from this rule.
  6. No lock may be left held when an exception is raised.

In a real interview there are no ready-made tests. Write a test yourself that proves that the Part 1 code, used as is from multiple threads, really does book the same slot to two people. It must reproduce on every run, not by luck; then use the same test to show that the new version does not have this problem.

Part 3 — Booking several resources at once

A meeting needs one room plus two GPUs, and can't happen if any one is missing. Add:

    def reserve_all(self, requests: list[tuple[str, int, int]], owner: str) -> int | None:
        """Book every (resource, start, end) in `requests`, or none of them.
        One booking id covers all of them."""
  • All or nothing. If any leg conflicts with an existing booking, return None and book nothing. Other threads must not see a "half-booked" intermediate state, nor be blocked by one.
  • The same resource may appear more than once in one request (e.g. the same room in the morning and the afternoon). If two legs within the request overlap each other, the whole request fails and returns None.
  • requests has 1 to 16 legs; raise ValueError if it is empty. If any leg has an invalid resource name or interval, raise as per the rules above and book nothing.
  • The whole request uses a single id. Each of its legs carries that id in query; cancel(id) cancels all legs at once and still takes effect exactly once.
  • reserve(r, s, e, owner) behaves exactly like reserve_all([(r, s, e)], owner).
  • No deadlock. If one thread calls reserve_all([("a", …), ("b", …)], …) while another simultaneously calls reserve_all([("b", …), ("a", …)], …), both calls must return.
  • All the Part 2 requirements still hold. Rule 5 becomes: two requests whose resources don't intersect must not wait on each other.
svc = ReservationService(["gpu-0", "gpu-1", "room-a"])
svc.reserve("gpu-1", 5, 8, "ann")                               -> 1
svc.reserve_all([("gpu-0", 0, 10), ("gpu-1", 0, 5)], "bob")     -> 2      # on gpu-1, [0,5) touches [5,8)
svc.reserve_all([("room-a", 0, 4), ("gpu-1", 7, 9)], "cat")     -> None   # conflicts with 1 on gpu-1
svc.query("room-a", 0, 100)                                     -> []     # so room-a was not booked either
svc.reserve_all([("room-a", 0, 4), ("room-a", 3, 6)], "cat")    -> None   # its own two legs overlap
svc.reserve_all([("room-a", 0, 4), ("room-a", 4, 6)], "cat")    -> 3
svc.query("room-a", 0, 100)                                     -> [(0, 4, 3, "cat"), (4, 6, 3, "cat")]
svc.cancel(2)                                                   -> True
svc.query("gpu-0", 0, 100)                                      -> []
svc.query("gpu-1", 0, 100)                                      -> [(5, 8, 1, "ann")]
solution:
The three parts are written as three classes: ReservationService (Part 1), ConcurrentReservationService (Part 2), and AtomicReservationService (Part 3). They are kept separate so that the Part 1 class can be taken unchanged into a multithreaded setting to show how it fails. In the interview, just modify one class step by step.

Part 1

Each resource keeps a list sorted by start, whose elements are (start, end, booking_id, owner). The intervals in the list are pairwise disjoint, so sorted by start means end is increasing too. Both operations rely on this:

  • Checking whether [start, end) is free. Any interval that could overlap it must start before end; those intervals form a prefix cal[:i] of the list, with i found by binary search. The last interval in the prefix has the largest end. If its end <= start, no interval in the prefix reaches into [start, end), so it is free; otherwise that interval itself overlaps [start, end). So only the single interval cal[i-1] needs checking.
  • Querying the intervals that overlap [start, end). "Starts before end" is a prefix and "ends after start" is a suffix; two binary searches give their intersection, a contiguous slice.

The binary search uses a small trick of tuple comparison: (end,) is smaller than any longer tuple starting with end, so bisect_left(cal, (end,)) is exactly "the first position with start >= end."

Complexity: the conflict check takes O(logn) comparisons. Insertion and deletion locate their position by binary search, but a Python list has to shift the elements after it, so the worst case is O(n) (a single memory move, still fast when n is in the tens of thousands; strict O(logn) needs a balanced tree or a structure like sortedcontainers). A query is O(logn+k), where k is the number of results returned.

The code deliberately splits "check" and "write" into two steps (_commit, _uncommit). The gap between these two steps is exactly what Part 2 has to protect, and it is also where the tests attack.

import bisect
import threading
from contextlib import contextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass
class Booking:
    id: int
    owner: str
    legs: tuple                  # ((resource, start, end), ...)
    active: bool = True          # guarded by the locks of the resources in legs


def check_interval(start, end):
    if start >= end:
        raise ValueError(f"empty interval [{start}, {end})")


def is_free(cal, start, end):
    """cal: sorted, pairwise disjoint [(start, end, booking_id, owner)]. True iff [start, end) hits none."""
    i = bisect.bisect_left(cal, (end,))          # cal[:i] are exactly the intervals that start before `end`
    return i == 0 or cal[i - 1][1] <= start      # disjoint + sorted: the last of them also ends last


def overlapping(cal, start, end):
    """The intervals of cal that overlap [start, end), as a new list (still sorted by start)."""
    lo = bisect.bisect_right(cal, start, key=lambda item: item[1])   # first interval that ends after `start`
    hi = bisect.bisect_left(cal, (end,))                              # first interval that starts at/after `end`
    return cal[lo:hi]


def remove_leg(cal, start, end, booking_id):
    i = bisect.bisect_left(cal, (start, end, booking_id))
    assert cal[i][:3] == (start, end, booking_id)
    del cal[i]


class ReservationService:
    """Part 1: correct for one caller at a time. No locks."""

    def __init__(self, resources):
        self._cal = {name: [] for name in resources}     # resource -> sorted [(start, end, booking_id, owner)]
        self._bookings = {}                              # booking_id -> Booking, active ones only
        self._next_id = 1

    def reserve(self, resource, start, end, owner):
        cal = self._cal[resource]                        # KeyError for an unknown resource
        check_interval(start, end)
        if not is_free(cal, start, end):                 # check ...
            return None
        return self._commit(owner, ((resource, start, end),))    # ... then act

    def _commit(self, owner, legs):
        booking = Booking(self._next_id, owner, legs)
        self._next_id += 1
        self._bookings[booking.id] = booking
        for resource, start, end in legs:
            bisect.insort(self._cal[resource], (start, end, booking.id, owner))
        return booking.id

    def cancel(self, booking_id):
        booking = self._bookings.get(booking_id)
        if booking is None:                              # check ...
            return False
        self._uncommit(booking)                          # ... then act
        return True

    def _uncommit(self, booking):
        del self._bookings[booking.id]
        for resource, start, end in booking.legs:
            remove_leg(self._cal[resource], start, end, booking.id)

    def query(self, resource, start, end):
        cal = self._cal[resource]
        check_interval(start, end)
        return overlapping(cal, start, end)

Part 2

Why the Part 1 code is wrong under multiple threads. reserve is check-then-act. Thread A checks and finds the slot free, but before it writes, thread B checks too and also finds it free, so both write and the same slot is booked to two people. cancel is the same: both threads see "the booking is still there" and both delete it. self._next_id += 1 is three steps, "read, add, write," so two threads may read the same value. CPython's global interpreter lock (GIL) only guarantees that a single bytecode instruction is not interrupted, not a sequence of operations, so it doesn't help. It's just that this gap is usually only a few microseconds wide, and a casually written stress test will probably never hit it, which is exactly what makes this kind of bug dangerous.

What must be atomic, and which lock protects it:

Shared state Protected by
A resource's booking list _cal[r]; "check free + insert" as a whole That resource's lock _locks[r]
Booking.active; "check still active + delete" as a whole The locks of the resources the booking involves
The id counter _next_id, the id index _bookings The small lock _meta
  • One lock per resource. Operations on different resources take different locks and don't wait on each other. All locks are created at once in the constructor: if they were "created on first use," creating the lock would itself be another check-then-act.
  • _meta is always taken last. _meta is only ever taken while already holding resource locks; while holding _meta no other lock is ever taken, and it is released after just a few assignments. With a fixed locking order, there is no deadlock.
  • cancel has to "look up, then lock, then confirm." With only an id you don't know which resource to lock, so first look up the booking under _meta, release _meta, then take the resource lock. There is a gap between the lookup and the lock, and another thread may already have cancelled it, so after taking the resource lock you must check booking.active once more.
  • Why not just pop under _meta to decide whose cancel succeeds? That would still give "exactly one True," but it allows this ordering: thread A's pop succeeds, but it hasn't yet removed the interval from the list; thread B's cancel gets False and returns; B then reserves the same slot and gets None, because the interval is still there. B was just told "it's already cancelled," yet can't book the slot, which violates rule 3. Putting the "is it still active" check and the removal of the interval under the same resource lock avoids this problem.
  • query must take the resource lock too, otherwise it might binary-search a list that is halfway through being modified. It returns a slice, i.e. a new list holding immutable tuples, so whatever others do after the lock is released doesn't affect it.
  • Argument checks happen before taking locks; locks are always taken with with, so they are released when an exception is raised.

How to test it. The race window is too narrow, so widen it in the test. Write a subclass that overrides _commit and pauses just before the actual write. The pause is a threading.Barrier(8): only after all 8 threads have passed the check and are all waiting there are they released together. So it is not "possibly" wrong; every time, all 8 threads get an id. Do the same with the locked version: only one thread can be in the critical section at a time, so the 8 can never all gather; the first thread times out and carries on, and the other 7 then see the slot taken and get None. That is exactly what the verification code below does. Rule 5 (different resources don't wait on each other) is tested the same way: 6 threads each book a different resource, and they are required to all be paused inside their critical sections at the same time.

class ConcurrentReservationService:
    """Part 2: one lock per resource; a small inner lock for the id counter and the id index."""

    def __init__(self, resources):
        self._cal = {name: [] for name in resources}
        self._locks = {name: threading.Lock() for name in self._cal}    # all created here, never lazily
        self._bookings = {}
        self._next_id = 1
        self._meta = threading.Lock()        # guards _bookings and _next_id; always the innermost lock

    def reserve(self, resource, start, end, owner):
        lock = self._locks[resource]                     # KeyError before any lock is taken
        check_interval(start, end)
        with lock:                                       # check and insert are one atomic step
            if not is_free(self._cal[resource], start, end):
                return None
            return self._commit(owner, ((resource, start, end),))

    def _commit(self, owner, legs):
        """Caller holds the lock of every resource in legs."""
        with self._meta:
            booking = Booking(self._next_id, owner, legs)
            self._next_id += 1
            self._bookings[booking.id] = booking
        for resource, start, end in legs:
            bisect.insort(self._cal[resource], (start, end, booking.id, owner))
        return booking.id

    def cancel(self, booking_id):
        with self._meta:
            booking = self._bookings.get(booking_id)
        if booking is None:
            return False
        with self._locks[booking.legs[0][0]]:
            if not booking.active:                       # another cancel got in between the lookup and the lock
                return False
            self._uncommit(booking)
        return True

    def _uncommit(self, booking):
        """Caller holds the lock of every resource in booking.legs."""
        booking.active = False
        for resource, start, end in booking.legs:
            remove_leg(self._cal[resource], start, end, booking.id)
        with self._meta:
            del self._bookings[booking.id]

    def query(self, resource, start, end):
        lock = self._locks[resource]
        check_interval(start, end)
        with lock:
            return overlapping(self._cal[resource], start, end)      # a slice: a private copy of immutable tuples

Part 3

First, think through how it would deadlock. A request involving several resources has to hold all their locks at once to make "check all + write all" atomic. If locks are taken in the order the request lists them, thread 1 takes a and waits for b, thread 2 takes b and waits for a, and neither ever lets go.

The fix: everyone takes locks in the same global order. Here, sorted by resource name. Then every lock a thread waits for comes after all the locks it already holds. A deadlock needs a cycle of threads that closes on itself; walking around that cycle, the lock names would have to keep increasing and yet return to the start, which is impossible.

Three details:

  • Deduplicate. The same resource can appear twice in a request, and threading.Lock is not reentrant: a thread that takes it a second time deadlocks itself. Hence sorted(set(...)).
  • Check everything first, then write everything. After acquiring all the locks, first confirm every leg is free, then confirm the legs within the request don't overlap each other (sort the legs and compare only adjacent pairs), and only start writing once everything passes. On failure nothing has been written yet, so no rollback is needed. The alternative is to insert as you check and undo on failure; as long as all the locks are held throughout, others still can't see the intermediate state, but there is an extra undo path that is easy to get wrong.
  • Release. In try/finally, release only the locks actually acquired. Release order doesn't affect correctness.

cancel also has to take all the resource locks the booking involves, in the same order. reserve, as in Part 2, involves only one lock.

For a request with m legs: sorting is O(mlogm), the check is O(mlogn) comparisons, and insertion is O(n) per leg in the worst case. When two requests' resources don't intersect, they take completely different locks and don't wait on each other.

class AtomicReservationService(ConcurrentReservationService):
    """Part 3: all-or-nothing bookings across several resources, locks taken in one global order."""

    def _lock_order(self, resources):
        return sorted(set(resources))        # set(): Lock is not reentrant; sorted(): the same order for everyone

    @contextmanager
    def _locked(self, resources):
        held = []
        try:
            for name in self._lock_order(resources):
                self._locks[name].acquire()
                held.append(name)
            yield
        finally:
            for name in reversed(held):
                self._locks[name].release()

    def reserve_all(self, requests, owner):
        legs = tuple((resource, start, end) for resource, start, end in requests)
        if not legs:
            raise ValueError("empty request")
        for resource, start, end in legs:                # validate everything before taking any lock
            self._locks[resource]
            check_interval(start, end)
        with self._locked([resource for resource, _, _ in legs]):
            if not self._all_free(legs):
                return None                              # nothing has been written yet: no rollback needed
            return self._commit(owner, legs)

    def _all_free(self, legs):
        if not all(is_free(self._cal[resource], start, end) for resource, start, end in legs):
            return False
        ordered = sorted(legs)                           # legs of one request must not hit each other either
        return all(a[0] != b[0] or a[2] <= b[1] for a, b in zip(ordered, ordered[1:]))

    def cancel(self, booking_id):
        with self._meta:
            booking = self._bookings.get(booking_id)
        if booking is None:
            return False
        with self._locked([resource for resource, _, _ in booking.legs]):
            if not booking.active:
                return False
            self._uncommit(booking)
        return True

Follow-up questions

With the GIL, why do we still need locks? The GIL ensures "only one thread executes bytecode at any moment," but the interpreter switches threads between bytecode instructions (by default it asks the running thread to yield every 5 milliseconds). Between the check and the write there are dozens of bytecode instructions and several function calls, and a switch landing in the middle is a bug. Single operations like list.append and dict.pop happen to be atomic in CPython, but relying on that is neither portable nor robust to code changes; and in free-threaded Python without the GIL (optional since 3.13), even that "happens to be" needs re-examining.

Would a single global lock work? Yes, and it is the hardest to get wrong; Part 3 wouldn't need to think about locking order either. The cost is that every operation queues up. For purely in-memory operations the critical section is only a few microseconds, and the GIL already serializes CPU work, so splitting into one lock per resource buys almost no throughput. Splitting locks really pays off when the critical section contains I/O (writing logs, writing to a database), or with a truly parallel runtime. In the interview, state this trade-off first, then split the locks as the problem requires. When reads far outnumber writes, query can even go lock-free: the writer builds a new immutable list each time and swaps the reference as a whole, and readers use whichever version they got.

How do you test concurrency bugs? What does a passing test tell you? Use two kinds of test together. One is deterministic: insert pause points where you suspect a gap, and use a Barrier to force the worst interleaving, as above, so it reproduces every time. The other is a stress test: many threads do random operations, and afterwards you check the invariants (no overlaps on any resource, ids are exactly 1..K, each id is successfully cancelled at most once, the final state equals exactly "issued minus cancelled"); you can also record the order of every call and check whether two overlapping bookings ever existed at the same time. During stress tests, add a very short sleep inside the critical section, or call sys.setswitchinterval(1e-6), and thread switches become much more frequent. But a passing test only says "the interleavings we tried didn't fail." So you still need the table above, "which lock protects each piece of shared state," to make the argument; tests are just for catching holes in the argument.

What if the service runs as several processes, on several machines? An in-process lock only works within one process; the invariant has to be enforced by the storage everyone shares. Common approaches:

  • Database constraints. PostgreSQL's exclusion constraint can directly express "time ranges on the same resource don't overlap": EXCLUDE USING gist (resource WITH =, during WITH &&), where during is a range type (such as tstzrange, which is half-open by default), and using = on a plain scalar column requires the btree_gist extension. An insert that violates the constraint raises an error, which the application translates to "already taken." On a database without such constraints, you can cut time into fixed-length slots and put a unique index on (resource, slot).
  • Pessimistic locking. In one transaction, first lock the resource's row in the resources table with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, then check for conflicts, then insert. Locking the resource row is the safest: in PostgreSQL, locking only the existing booking rows you found does not stop someone else from inserting a new one. When booking several resources at once, lock the rows in a fixed order, for the same reason as in Part 3; when the database detects a deadlock it rolls back one of the transactions, and the application must be ready to retry.
  • Optimistic concurrency. Put a version number on the resource row. Read version v, check for conflicts, then in the same transaction insert the booking and run UPDATE … SET version = v + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = v. If zero rows are affected, someone got there first: roll back, re-read, and retry. Fast when conflicts are rare; on a hot resource it retries over and over.
  • Just "first SELECT to check for conflicts, then INSERT" is wrong under the default isolation level, exactly the same race as in Part 1. PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level can detect this conflict and end one of the transactions with a serialization failure (SQLSTATE 40001), which the application must retry; its REPEATABLE READ (snapshot isolation) does not prevent it.
  • A distributed lock using something like Redis also works, but such locks come with leases: if the holder stalls briefly, the lock may already have expired without it knowing. So the write side still needs a database constraint, or a check on a monotonically increasing fencing token.

Can a client retrying after a timeout cause problems? Yes. The request actually succeeded, but the response was lost. When the client retries, it finds the slot taken (by its own previous attempt), gets None, concludes it didn't get the booking, and leaves behind a booking nobody claims. The fix is an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key for each logical request and sends the same key on retries; the server writes "key → result" in the same transaction as the booking itself, with a unique constraint on the key. When it sees the same key again it doesn't re-execute, it just returns the stored result. Three more things to handle: two requests with the same key arriving at once (the unique constraint makes the later one wait or fail, then read the existing result); the same key with different parameters (reject); and how long to keep keys.

What about "hold the slot first, confirm within N seconds, otherwise release automatically"? Give bookings a status and an expiry time: hold(...) creates a provisional booking with expires_at, and confirm(id) turns it into a confirmed one. The key is to make every decision under the resource lock: when checking whether a slot is free, treat expired holds as nonexistent and delete them while you're there; confirm checks "not yet expired" and changes the status under the same lock. That way you never get "confirm returned success, but the slot has already gone to someone else." Judge expiry with a monotonic clock (time.monotonic), and make the clock an injectable parameter so tests can use a fake clock instead of actually calling sleep. In a database this is usually a status column plus expires_at, with a cleanup job marking expired records as released, and the exclusion constraint applying only to unreleased rows (add a WHERE clause to the constraint).

Verification code (runnable) 
import itertools
import random
import threading
import time

HORIZON = 10 ** 9


def expect_raises(exc, fn, *args):
    try:
        fn(*args)
    except exc:
        return
    raise AssertionError(f"{fn.__name__}{args} did not raise {exc.__name__}")


def run_threads(targets, timeout=60.0):
    """Start one daemon thread per callable, wait for all; fail loudly instead of hanging."""
    threads = [threading.Thread(target=t, daemon=True) for t in targets]
    for t in threads:
        t.start()
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
    for t in threads:
        t.join(max(0.0, deadline - time.monotonic()))
    assert not any(t.is_alive() for t in threads), "threads are stuck"


# ---------- 1. the statement's examples (one caller) ----------

# ---------- 2. one caller, random operations, against a model that only scans lists ----------
class ScanModel:
    def __init__(self, resources):
        self.resources = set(resources)
        self.active = {}                       # id -> (owner, legs)
        self.issued = 0

    def reserve_all(self, requests, owner):
        legs = list(requests)
        taken = [leg for _, booked in self.active.values() for leg in booked]
        for i, (r, s, e) in enumerate(legs):
            if any(r == r2 and s < e2 and s2 < e for r2, s2, e2 in taken + legs[:i]):
                return None
        self.issued += 1
        self.active[self.issued] = (owner, legs)
        return self.issued

    def cancel(self, booking_id):
        return self.active.pop(booking_id, None) is not None

    def query(self, resource, start, end):
        return sorted((s, e, bid, owner) for bid, (owner, legs) in self.active.items()
                      for r, s, e in legs if r == resource and s < end and start < e)


def random_leg(rng, names, span=30):
    start = rng.randrange(span)
    return rng.choice(names), start, start + rng.randint(1, 6)


for cls in (ReservationService, ConcurrentReservationService, AtomicReservationService):
    rng = random.Random(2026)
    for _ in range(150):
        names = ["r%d" % i for i in range(rng.randint(1, 3))]
        svc, model = cls(names), ScanModel(names)
        for _ in range(80):
            p = rng.random()
            if p < 0.45:
                leg = random_leg(rng, names)
                assert svc.reserve(*leg, "u") == model.reserve_all([leg], "u")
            elif p < 0.60 and cls is AtomicReservationService:
                legs = [random_leg(rng, names) for _ in range(rng.randint(1, 3))]
                assert svc.reserve_all(legs, "v") == model.reserve_all(legs, "v")
            elif p < 0.80:
                bid = rng.randint(1, model.issued + 2)
                assert svc.cancel(bid) == model.cancel(bid)
            else:
                r, s, e = random_leg(rng, names)
                assert svc.query(r, s, e) == model.query(r, s, e)
        for r in names:
            assert svc.query(r, 0, HORIZON) == model.query(r, 0, HORIZON)
        assert sorted(svc._bookings) == sorted(model.active)


# ---------- 3. the race, made deterministic ----------
def paused(cls, pause):
    """cls with pause() called in the gap between a check and the write that follows it."""
    class Paused(cls):
        def _commit(self, owner, legs):          # reserve: after "is it free?", before the insert
            pause()
            return super()._commit(owner, legs)

        def _uncommit(self, booking):            # cancel: after "is it still there?", before the removal
            pause()
            return super()._uncommit(booking)
    return Paused


def meeting_point(n, wait):
    """pause() that blocks until n threads are in it together; gives up after `wait` seconds.
    Returns (pause, gave_up) where gave_up collects one item per thread that gave up."""
    gate, gave_up = threading.Barrier(n), []

    def pause():
        try:
            gate.wait(timeout=wait)
        except threading.BrokenBarrierError:
            gave_up.append(1)
    return pause, gave_up


def same_slot_race(cls, wait, n=8):
    """n threads book the same slot; each is held after its check until all n have passed theirs."""
    pause, _ = meeting_point(n, wait)
    svc = paused(cls, pause)(["room"])
    results = []                                 # list.append is atomic in CPython; good enough for a harness
    run_threads([lambda i=i: results.append(svc.reserve("room", 10, 20, f"user{i}")) for i in range(n)])
    return results, svc.query("room", 0, HORIZON)


# Part 1 code called from 8 threads. Nothing stops all 8 from passing the check, so the gate fills at once
# (the 30 s is only a safety net) and every caller is told the slot is theirs.
results, cal = same_slot_race(ReservationService, wait=30.0)
assert results.count(None) == 0 and len(cal) == 8
assert all(item[:2] == (10, 20) for item in cal)
print("no locks:", len(cal), "bookings of room [10, 20) at the same time")

# With the lock only one thread can be between check and insert, so the gate can never fill: the first
# thread gives up after 0.3 s, books, and the other seven then see the slot taken.
for cls in (ConcurrentReservationService, AtomicReservationService):
    results, cal = same_slot_race(cls, wait=0.3)
    assert sorted(results, key=str) == [1] + [None] * 7 and len(cal) == 1


# ---------- 4. different resources really do not wait for each other ----------
def together_in_critical_section(cls, wait, n=6):
    """n threads book n different resources; each pauses inside its critical section until all n are inside.
    Returns how many gave up waiting (0 means all n critical sections were open at the same moment)."""
    pause, gave_up = meeting_point(n, wait)
    svc = paused(cls, pause)([f"r{i}" for i in range(n)])
    results = []
    run_threads([lambda i=i: results.append(svc.reserve(f"r{i}", 0, 1, "u")) for i in range(n)])
    assert sorted(results) == list(range(1, n + 1))
    return len(gave_up)


class GlobalLockService(ConcurrentReservationService):
    """Negative control: every resource shares one lock."""
    def __init__(self, resources):
        super().__init__(resources)
        one = threading.Lock()
        self._locks = {name: one for name in self._cal}


assert together_in_critical_section(ConcurrentReservationService, wait=30.0) == 0
assert together_in_critical_section(AtomicReservationService, wait=30.0) == 0
assert together_in_critical_section(GlobalLockService, wait=0.3) == 6      # the test can tell the difference


# ---------- 5. one booking, many cancels: exactly one True ----------
class NoLock:
    def acquire(self):
        return True

    def release(self):
        pass

    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        pass


class UnsynchronisedService(AtomicReservationService):
    """The Part 3 reference with every lock replaced by a no-op: the deliberately broken version."""
    def __init__(self, resources):
        super().__init__(resources)
        self._locks = {name: NoLock() for name in self._cal}
        self._meta = NoLock()


def cancel_race(cls, wait, n=8):
    """n threads cancel the same booking; each is held after its "still there?" check until all n passed."""
    pause, _ = meeting_point(n, wait)
    svc = cls(["a", "b"])                        # book first, without any pause ...
    bid = svc.reserve("a", 0, 5, "u")
    svc.__class__ = paused(cls, pause)           # ... then switch the pauses on for the cancels
    answers = []

    def cancel_once():
        try:
            answers.append(svc.cancel(bid))
        except Exception as exc:
            answers.append(type(exc).__name__)

    run_threads([cancel_once] * n)
    return answers


for cls in (ReservationService, UnsynchronisedService):         # no locks: all 8 pass the check, then all 8 act
    answers = cancel_race(cls, wait=30.0)
    assert answers.count(True) + answers.count(False) < 8 or answers.count(True) > 1, answers
    print("no locks, 8 cancels of one booking:", sorted(answers, key=str))
for cls in (ConcurrentReservationService, AtomicReservationService):
    assert sorted(cancel_race(cls, wait=0.3)) == [False] * 7 + [True]

for cls in (ConcurrentReservationService, AtomicReservationService):       # and without any pause, many times
    for _ in range(30):
        svc = cls(["a", "b"])
        bid = svc.reserve("a", 0, 5, "u")
        if cls is AtomicReservationService:
            bid = svc.reserve_all([("a", 5, 9), ("b", 0, 9)], "u")
        start, answers = threading.Barrier(8), []

        def cancel_once():
            start.wait()
            answers.append(svc.cancel(bid))

        run_threads([cancel_once] * 8)
        assert sorted(answers) == [False] * 7 + [True]
        assert svc.query("b", 0, 99) == [] and bid not in svc._bookings


# ---------- 6. two callers, two resources, opposite order ----------
class ProbeLock:
    """Stands in for a Lock. Gives up after `timeout` seconds instead of waiting forever, and
    calls after_acquire() each time it has been taken."""
    def __init__(self, timeout, after_acquire):
        self._lock, self._timeout, self._after = threading.Lock(), timeout, after_acquire

    def acquire(self):
        if not self._lock.acquire(timeout=self._timeout):
            raise TimeoutError("still waiting for a lock")
        self._after()

    def release(self):
        self._lock.release()

    def __enter__(self):
        self.acquire()

    def __exit__(self, *exc):
        self.release()


class RequestOrderService(AtomicReservationService):
    """The tempting version: take the locks in the order the request lists them."""
    def _lock_order(self, resources):
        return list(dict.fromkeys(resources))


def opposite_orders(cls, lock_timeout, gate_timeout):
    """Thread 1 books (a, b), thread 2 books (b, a), different hours. After its first lock each thread
    waits at a gate until the other one also holds a lock (or until gate_timeout)."""
    gate, first = threading.Barrier(2), threading.local()

    def after_acquire():
        if getattr(first, "done", False):
            return
        first.done = True
        try:
            gate.wait(timeout=gate_timeout)
        except threading.BrokenBarrierError:
            pass

    svc = cls(["a", "b"])
    svc._locks = {name: ProbeLock(lock_timeout, after_acquire) for name in svc._locks}
    outcome = []

    def book(legs, owner):
        try:
            outcome.append(svc.reserve_all(legs, owner))
        except TimeoutError:
            outcome.append("deadlock")

    run_threads([lambda: book([("a", 0, 1), ("b", 0, 1)], "t1"), lambda: book([("b", 5, 6), ("a", 5, 6)], "t2")])
    return outcome


# With the gate both threads hold their first lock before either asks for its second one, so neither
# request can be granted until somebody gives up: the timeout below is not a guess about speed.
outcome = opposite_orders(RequestOrderService, lock_timeout=1.0, gate_timeout=10.0)
assert "deadlock" in outcome, outcome
print("request-order locking:", outcome)
# Sorted order: both want "a" first, so they can never each hold one lock. The gate times out, nobody is stuck.
outcome = opposite_orders(AtomicReservationService, lock_timeout=30.0, gate_timeout=0.2)
assert sorted(outcome) == [1, 2], outcome


# ---------- 7. the storm ----------
class Ticker:
    """A logical clock shared by all threads."""
    def __init__(self):
        self._lock, self._now = threading.Lock(), 0

    def tick(self):
        with self._lock:
            self._now += 1
            return self._now


def storm(svc, n_threads=12, n_ops=250, seed=0, span=120):
    """Random reserve / reserve_all / cancel / query from n_threads threads. Returns a dict of problem counts."""
    names = sorted(svc._cal)
    ticker, pool_lock = Ticker(), threading.Lock()
    pool = []                                    # ids anyone may try to cancel
    logs = [dict(issued=[], cancelled=[], errors=[], bad_snapshots=0) for _ in range(n_threads)]

    def worker(k):
        rng, log = random.Random(seed * 1000 + k), logs[k]
        for _ in range(n_ops):
            p = rng.random()
            try:
                if p < 0.40:
                    legs = [random_leg(rng, names, span)]
                    bid = svc.reserve(*legs[0], f"t{k}")
                elif p < 0.60:
                    legs = [random_leg(rng, names, span) for _ in range(rng.randint(2, 3))]
                    bid = svc.reserve_all(legs, f"t{k}")
                elif p < 0.90:
                    with pool_lock:
                        victim = rng.choice(pool) if pool else 0
                    before = ticker.tick()                       # taken before the call starts
                    if svc.cancel(victim):
                        log["cancelled"].append((victim, before))
                    continue
                else:
                    r, s, e = random_leg(rng, names, span)
                    snap = svc.query(r, 0, HORIZON)
                    if any(a[1] > b[0] for a, b in zip(snap, snap[1:])) or snap != sorted(snap):
                        log["bad_snapshots"] += 1
                    continue
                if bid is not None:
                    log["issued"].append((bid, legs, ticker.tick()))     # tick taken after the call returned
                    with pool_lock:
                        pool.append(bid)
            except Exception as exc:                             # only the broken version gets here
                log["errors"].append(repr(exc))

    run_threads([lambda k=k: worker(k) for k in range(n_threads)], timeout=120.0)

    issued = [x for log in logs for x in log["issued"]]
    cancelled = [x for log in logs for x in log["cancelled"]]
    ids = sorted(bid for bid, _, _ in issued)
    cancelled_ids = [bid for bid, _ in cancelled]
    problems = dict(
        errors=sum(len(log["errors"]) for log in logs),
        bad_snapshots=sum(log["bad_snapshots"] for log in logs),
        ids_not_1_to_k=int(ids != list(range(1, len(ids) + 1))),
        cancelled_twice=len(cancelled_ids) - len(set(cancelled_ids)),
    )
    # (a) what is left must be exactly: everything issued and not cancelled
    gone = set(cancelled_ids)
    expected = {name: [] for name in names}
    for bid, legs, _ in issued:
        if bid not in gone:
            for r, s, e in legs:
                expected[r].append((s, e, bid))
    final = {name: [item[:3] for item in svc.query(name, 0, HORIZON)] for name in names}
    problems["final_state_wrong"] = sum(final[name] != sorted(expected[name]) for name in names)
    problems["final_overlaps"] = sum(1 for name in names for a, b in itertools.combinations(final[name], 2)
                                     if a[0] < b[1] and b[0] < a[1])
    problems["index_wrong"] = int(sorted(svc._bookings) != sorted(set(ids) - gone))
    # (b) double bookings that were cancelled again before the end: booking X certainly existed from the
    # tick after its reserve returned until the tick before its successful cancel started. Two bookings
    # that overlap on a resource must never have certainly existed at the same tick.
    end_tick = dict(cancelled)
    alive = [(r, s, e, born, end_tick.get(bid, float("inf"))) for bid, legs, born in issued for r, s, e in legs]
    by_resource = {name: [x for x in alive if x[0] == name] for name in names}
    problems["double_booked_pairs"] = sum(
        1 for name in names for a, b in itertools.combinations(by_resource[name], 2)
        if a[1] < b[2] and b[1] < a[2] and a[3] < b[4] and b[3] < a[4])
    return problems, len(ids), len(cancelled_ids)


def yield_a_little():
    time.sleep(0.0002)       # lets other threads run in the middle of the critical section


RESOURCES = ["r0", "r1", "r2", "r3"]
for seed in range(3):
    problems, n_issued, n_cancelled = storm(paused(AtomicReservationService, yield_a_little)(RESOURCES), seed=seed)
    assert not any(problems.values()), problems
    assert n_issued > 200 and n_cancelled > 100            # the storm really did book and cancel a lot
    print("storm, reference:", n_issued, "bookings,", n_cancelled, "cancels, no problems")

problems, n_issued, n_cancelled = storm(paused(UnsynchronisedService, yield_a_little)(RESOURCES), seed=0)
assert problems["double_booked_pairs"] > 0, problems       # the same storm catches the version without locks
print("storm, no locks:", problems)
print("all checks passed")
